solution.concept_anchor: Mapping constitutional innovations to their originating Act
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is deceptive because it correctly places dyarchy under 1919 but incorrectly assigns bicameral central legislature to 1909, exploiting the fact that the 1909 Act did significantly modify the Imperial Legislative Council.
elimination_logic: Match A (Dyarchy at provincial level): This was the defining innovation of the 1919 Act — match A-1.
Match B (Single-chamber Imperial Legislative Council): The Morley-Minto 1909 Act created/modified this single-chamber body — match B-2.
Match C (Bicameral central legislature): Bicameralism at the Centre was introduced by the 1919 Act — match C-1.
Match D (Separate electorates for Muslims only): The 1909 Act introduced this; the 1919 Act extended it to more communities — match D-2.
Correct combination: A-1, B-2, C-1, D-2 — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges two 1909 Act features with 1919 Act innovations. Because the 1909 Act was also a landmark reform, students sometimes attribute early elected-representation milestones to 1919 and vice versa. The key distinguishing facts: (1) bicameralism at the Centre belongs exclusively to 1919, (2) separate electorates for Muslims alone belongs to 1909.
solution.final_explanation:
This question requires clean separation of which constitutional innovation belongs to which Act.

Correct matches:
• A (Dyarchy at provincial level) → 1919 Act: Dyarchy was the signature innovation of the Government of India Act 1919 — no prior Act had this feature.
• B (Single-chamber Imperial Legislative Council) → 1909 Act: The Morley-Minto reforms expanded the Imperial Legislative Council but kept it as a single body. Bicameralism came only in 1919.
• C (Bicameral central legislature) → 1919 Act: The Council of State and Central Legislative Assembly as a two-house central legislature were created by the 1919 Act for the first time.
• D (Separate electorates for Muslims only, no other community) → 1909 Act: The Morley-Minto Act introduced separate electorates exclusively for Muslims. The 1919 Act extended this to Sikhs, Anglo-Indians, Europeans, and Indian Christians.

Trap pairings: Options that assign bicameral central legislature to 1909 — incorrect, the 1909 Act retained a single chamber. Options that assign Muslim-only separate electorates to 1919 — incorrect, 1919 extended to multiple communities.

Value Addition:
• The 1909 Act is also called the Indian Councils Act 1909 — not the 'Government of India Act 1909.'
• The principle of separate electorates introduced in 1909 had profound consequences — it was eventually extended, challenged through the Communal Award (1932), and modified by the Poona Pact.
• Bicameralism at the Centre remained a feature through the 1935 Act and into the 1950 Constitution.

solution.concept_anchor: Non-Cooperation Movement 1920: scope of boycott programme
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is deceptive because foreign cloth boycott is so commonly associated with Gandhi's programmes broadly that students automatically assume it was part of Non-Cooperation, when it became a primary plank of Civil Disobedience (1930) rather than Non-Cooperation (1920).
elimination_logic: Identify what formally constituted the Non-Cooperation Movement's (1920) boycott programme: legislative councils, government schools/colleges, courts using British law, and British titles/honours.

Option (a) — Foreign cloth boycott: This was a major plank of Civil Disobedience Movement (1930), not Non-Cooperation (1920). The 1920 programme focused on institutional boycott (councils, courts, schools), not specifically foreign cloth.
Option (b) — Boycott of legislative councils: Explicitly part of Non-Cooperation 1920 — Congress refused to participate in the reformed councils. Belongs with the others.
Option (c) — Boycott of government educational institutions: Explicitly part of Non-Cooperation — students were urged to leave government schools and colleges. Belongs.
Option (d) — Boycott of British law courts: Explicitly part of Non-Cooperation — lawyers were urged to stop practicing in British courts. Belongs.
Option (a) does not belong — it is the odd one out. Select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap substitutes Civil Disobedience's hallmark (foreign cloth boycott) into the Non-Cooperation Movement's programme. Because Gandhi is associated with swadeshi and cloth-burning across multiple movements, students conflate the specific programmes of different agitations. The Non-Cooperation Movement's boycott was primarily institutional — councils, courts, schools — while economic boycott of foreign goods became central to Civil Disobedience.
solution.final_explanation:
The Non-Cooperation Movement launched in 1920 had a specifically defined boycott programme, distinct from later Gandhian agitations.

• Option (a) — Foreign cloth boycott: This is the odd one out. While swadeshi was a recurring Gandhian theme, the foreign cloth boycott became the economic centrepiece of the Civil Disobedience Movement (1930). The Non-Cooperation Movement's (1920) programme focused on institutional withdrawal, not primarily economic boycott of foreign goods.
• Option (b) — Boycott of legislative councils: This was explicitly part of the 1920 programme. Congress boycotted the reformed councils under the Government of India Act 1919, which the Swarajists later reversed in 1923.
• Option (c) — Boycott of government educational institutions: Students were called to leave government schools and colleges. National institutions like Jamia Millia Islamia and Kashi Vidyapith were founded as alternatives.
• Option (d) — Boycott of British law courts: Lawyers, including Motilal Nehru and C.R. Das, gave up legal practice as part of this commitment.

Value Addition:
• Non-Cooperation also included returning British honours and titles.
• The movement was suspended following the Chauri Chaura violence (February 1922), when a mob burned a police station, killing constables.
• The Swarajist reversal of the council boycott in 1923 showed that even within the nationalist movement, the institutional boycott strategy had limits.

solution.concept_anchor: Central legislature composition and Viceroy's legislative powers

statement_analysis.statement: Under the Government of India Act 1919, the Central Legislative Assembly had 145 members of whom 105 were elected, constituting the Lower House of the bicameral central legislature.
statement_analysis.reason: The Central Legislative Assembly (Lower House) had 145 total members with 105 elected — and it was indeed the Lower House of the bicameral structure introduced by the 1919 Act.

statement_analysis.statement: The Viceroy could not dissolve the Central Legislative Assembly before its term expired, as dissolution power was reserved exclusively for the Secretary of State acting through the Crown.
statement_analysis.reason: The Viceroy retained the power to summon, prorogue, and dissolve the Central Legislative Assembly — he was not constrained to await the term's natural expiry. The dissolution power was not reserved for the Secretary of State.

statement_analysis.statement: A portion of the central budget under the 1919 Act was classified as 'non-votable', meaning the Central Legislative Assembly could discuss but not vote on that portion of government expenditure.
statement_analysis.reason: Non-votable budget items were a genuine feature — elected members could discuss these expenditures but could not reduce or reject them through a vote, limiting the legislature's financial authority significantly.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) is deceptive for students who assume the Viceroy's powers were comprehensively listed in civics textbooks but may not recall the specific dissolution power attribution.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: 145 members, 105 elected, Lower House — all accurate for the Central Legislative Assembly. Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: Dissolution power belonged to the Viceroy, not the Secretary of State. The claim that dissolution was 'reserved exclusively for the Secretary of State acting through the Crown' is incorrect. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: Non-votable budget items were a real constraint on the legislature's financial authority — discussed but not voted upon. Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses a partial-truth mechanism — it correctly identifies that the Crown's authority was involved in Indian governance but incorrectly attributes the specific dissolution power to the Secretary of State rather than the Viceroy. Students who know 'the Crown retained ultimate authority' may not catch the specific error in the attribution of dissolution power.
solution.final_explanation:
The Central Legislative Assembly and its powers under the 1919 Act are frequently tested for precise compositional and power-related details.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Central Legislative Assembly had 145 members (105 elected, 40 nominated/official) — the Lower House of the bicameral central legislature. These numbers are standard exam-relevant data points.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Viceroy himself held the power to summon, prorogue, and dissolve the Central Legislative Assembly. This power was not delegated to the Secretary of State. The Viceroy's legislative powers — certification, dissolution, ordinance — all resided with him, not the Secretary of State.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The non-votable budget was a significant constraint. Elected members could debate non-votable items but the vote mechanism — the legislature's primary tool of financial control — was denied to them on a substantial portion of expenditure.

Value Addition:
• The Council of State (Upper House) had 60 members, 27 elected — smaller and more conservative than the Assembly.
• Both chambers were subordinate to the Viceroy — they could not remove him or his Council.
• The combination of non-votable budget + Viceroy's certification + ordinance power made the central legislature closer to a debating forum than a governing body.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is deceptive because it places the Communal Award (1932) before the Poona Pact (1932) — both occurred in 1932, and students who know one preceded the other within that year but are uncertain of the month may select this.
elimination_logic: Identify the chronological sequence of communal representation milestones.
Indian Councils Act 1909: introduced separate electorates for Muslims — the origin point.
Government of India Act 1919: extended separate electorates to Sikhs, Anglo-Indians, Europeans, Indian Christians.
Communal Award (August 1932): Ramsay MacDonald's award proposed separate electorates for Depressed Classes among others.
Poona Pact (September 1932): Gandhi's fast led to Poona Pact — separate electorates for Depressed Classes replaced by reserved seats in general electorates.
Correct sequence: 1909 Act → 1919 Act → Communal Award → Poona Pact. Select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap involves the Communal Award and Poona Pact — both 1932 events, one in August and one in September. Students who know the Poona Pact replaced the Communal Award may reverse their sequence, assuming the Pact preceded the Award. The causal chain is clear: Award first (the trigger) → Pact second (Gandhi's response).
solution.final_explanation:
The trajectory of communal representation in colonial India spans three decades and involves four key milestones.

Correct sequence:
1. Indian Councils Act 1909 (Morley-Minto): Introduced separate electorates for Muslims — the first institutionalization of communal representation.
2. Government of India Act 1919: Extended separate electorates to Sikhs, Anglo-Indians, Europeans, and Indian Christians — widening the communal framework.
3. Communal Award (August 1932): Ramsay MacDonald's Award proposed separate electorates for Depressed Classes (Scheduled Castes), among other communities. Gandhi launched a fast-unto-death in protest.
4. Poona Pact (September 1932): The Agreement between Gandhi and Ambedkar replaced separate electorates for Depressed Classes with reserved seats in general electorates — a compromise that ended Gandhi's fast.

Why wrong options fail:
• Options reversing 1909 and 1919 ignore that Muslim separate electorates preceded the 1919 extension.
• Options placing Poona Pact before Communal Award reverse the causal sequence — the Pact was a response to the Award.

Value Addition:
• The Communal Award also confirmed separate electorates for Muslims, Sikhs, and other communities — not just Depressed Classes.
• The Poona Pact significantly increased the reserved seats for Depressed Classes compared to what the Communal Award had proposed.
• The Poona Pact is the origin of the reserved constituency system that persists in Indian elections today.

solution.concept_anchor: Lee Commission 1924 and Central PSC establishment 1926

statement_analysis.statement: The Government of India Act 1919 provided the statutory basis for a Central Public Service Commission, and this body was actually established in 1926 following the recommendation of the Lee Commission (1924).
statement_analysis.reason: All three elements — statutory provision (1919), implementation year (1926), and the Lee Commission's (1924) accelerating role — are factually accurate.

statement_analysis.statement: The Lee Commission recommended that recruitment to the Indian Civil Service be conducted exclusively through examinations held in India, ending all parallel recruitment from England.
statement_analysis.reason: The Lee Commission recommended simultaneous recruitment through examinations held both in England and in India — not exclusive Indian recruitment. Ending English examination as the primary route was an aspiration, not the Commission's specific recommendation.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is deceptive because Statement 1 is wholly correct with multiple verifiable elements, and students who confirm it may assume Statement 2's 'progressive' description of the Lee Commission is also accurate without checking the 'exclusively in India' qualifier.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Three elements — statutory basis (1919), establishment year (1926), Lee Commission trigger (1924). All accurate. Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: 'Exclusively in India' and 'ending all parallel recruitment from England' — the Lee Commission recommended simultaneous (parallel, not exclusive) recruitment. The 'exclusive India' claim is incorrect. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap is embedded in Statement 2 — using 'exclusively' where 'simultaneously' is the correct qualifier. Students who know the Lee Commission was a step toward Indianization and that it involved Indian examinations may not catch the crucial difference between simultaneous recruitment (both England and India) and exclusive recruitment (India only). The word 'exclusively' transforms a true fact into a false claim.
solution.final_explanation:
The genesis of the Central Public Service Commission involves three connected milestones that must be distinguished clearly.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Government of India Act 1919 was the first legislation to provide a statutory basis for a Public Service Commission at the Centre. However, the actual body was not established immediately — it came into existence in 1926, seven years later, after the Lee Commission (Royal Commission on Superior Civil Services in India, 1924) made specific recommendations for its establishment to systematize Indianization.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Lee Commission did not recommend ending English recruitment. It recommended simultaneous examination-based recruitment in both England and India, with a target of achieving a 50:50 British-to-Indian ratio over approximately 15 years. 'Exclusively in India' misrepresents the Commission's recommendation by removing the parallel England component.

Value Addition:
• The first Central Public Service Commission (1926) was chaired by Sir Ross Barker.
• The distinction between covenanted (ICS) and uncovenanted (Provincial Civil Services) services is important — Indianization proceeded faster in the latter.
• The Federal Public Service Commission under the 1935 Act and the eventual UPSC (Article 315, 1950) are the institutional successors.

solution.concept_anchor: Tilak's characterization of the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is deceptive because Annie Besant was also a prominent critic of the reforms and her Home Rule critique is well-known, leading students to associate the famous critical phrase with her rather than Tilak.
elimination_logic: The phrase 'unworthy of England to offer and India to accept' regarding the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms — identify the correct author.
Eliminate option (a): Annie Besant criticized the reforms through the Home Rule movement perspective but this specific phrase is not attributed to her.

Eliminate option (b): Gandhi's response was to initially engage with the reforms; his critique was expressed differently — through the Non-Cooperation Movement's launch after Khilafat and Jallianwala Bagh.
Confirm option (c): Bal Gangadhar Tilak is credited with the characterization 'unworthy of England to offer and India to accept' — expressing his rejection of the reforms as inadequate.
Eliminate option (d): C.R. Das was associated with the Swarajist strategy of entering councils to obstruct from within — not with this particular phrase of rejection.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap substitutes Annie Besant for Tilak — both were vocal critics of British policy, both associated with the Home Rule movement, and both expressed strong opposition to the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms. Students who associate criticism of British reforms with Besant (who was prominent and arrested in 1917) may attribute this phrase to her rather than Tilak.
solution.final_explanation:
The nationalist response to the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms ranged from qualified acceptance (Moderates) to outright rejection (Extremists/Tilak).

• Option (a): Annie Besant — Incorrect. Besant was a prominent critic through the Home Rule movement and found the reforms inadequate, but this specific phrase is not attributable to her.
• Option (b): Mahatma Gandhi — Incorrect. Gandhi's critique of British policy in 1919–1920 focused on Jallianwala Bagh, the Rowlatt Act, and the Khilafat question — he did not use this specific formulation about the reforms.
• Option (c): Bal Gangadhar Tilak — Correct. Tilak articulated the assessment that the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms were 'unworthy of England to offer and India to accept,' encapsulating the extremist nationalist rejection of incremental reform as insulting to Indian political capacity.
• Option (d): C.R. Das — Incorrect. Das's response to the councils question was the Swarajist strategy — entering to obstruct — not a blanket rejection expressed in these terms.

Value Addition:
• Tilak died in August 1920, just before the Non-Cooperation Movement was formally launched — his assessment of the reforms shaped the movement's initial orientation.
• The Moderates (Liberal Federation under Surendranath Banerjea) took the opposite position, welcoming the reforms and participating from the start.
• The phrase encapsulates a recurring theme in colonial constitutional history: the gap between what was offered and what self-governance actually required.

solution.concept_anchor: Finance as reserved subject crippling dyarchy's transferred departments
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is deceptive because students who correctly identify A as true may question whether R is also true — wondering if perhaps finance was actually a shared subject rather than purely reserved. But R is factually accurate.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion A correct? A says dyarchy was criticized as unworkable because elected ministers lacked independent financial control. This is correct — the core critique of dyarchy was precisely that transferred subjects were unfunded.

Step 2 — Is Reason R correct? R says finance was classified as a reserved subject under the Devolution Rules 1920, meaning the Governor's Executive Council controlled fiscal allocations. This is correct — finance was reserved.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? Yes — R directly explains A. Finance being reserved meant elected ministers had to seek funds from the Governor's reserved executive for subjects they were responsible for. The financial dependency caused by R is the structural reason for the unworkability described in A.
Both A and R correct + R causally explains A — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation distractor in option (b) — 'both correct but R not the explanation' — tempts students who know that multiple factors contributed to dyarchy's failure, including the Governor's takeback power. They may reason that 'finance as reserved' is only one of many causes and therefore R is insufficient as an explanation. However, finance being reserved was the primary and direct structural cause identified by contemporaries and historians alike — R genuinely explains A.
solution.final_explanation:
The failure of dyarchy is one of the most analytically significant themes in the constitutional history of the 1919 reforms.

Assertion (A) analysis: Dyarchy was criticized from its implementation — the transferred ministers (responsible for education, health, agriculture) had legislative accountability but no financial autonomy. They could be held politically responsible for the state of public health but could not fund hospitals without the reserved executive's approval. A is correct.

Reason (R) analysis: Under the Devolution Rules 1920, finance was classified as a reserved subject administered by the Governor with his Executive Council of officials. Provincial governments could not independently access funds for transferred departments. R is correct.

Causal link: R is the direct structural cause of the problem A identifies. The reserved status of finance under the Devolution Rules (R) is precisely what made transferred ministers dependent on and vulnerable to the reserved executive, generating the unworkability criticism (A). The causal arrow runs directly from R to A.

Value Addition:
• Critics used the phrase 'responsible without power' to describe transferred ministers under dyarchy.
• The 1935 Act resolved this at the provincial level by giving ministers full fiscal authority — provincial autonomy meant real financial control.
• The devolution of fiscal authority remains a live federal tension in India's constitutional structure even today — the Finance Commission framework addresses a similar concern.

solution.concept_anchor: Dyarchy shifted to Centre under 1935 Act — never implemented
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is deceptive because students who know dyarchy was 'abolished at the provincial level' under 1935 may confuse this with a complete elimination of dyarchy from the constitutional framework, without knowing it was proposed (but never implemented) at the Centre.
elimination_logic: Track the fate of dyarchy from 1919 to 1935 and beyond.
Eliminate option (a): Dyarchy was not abolished entirely under the 1935 Act — it was proposed at the Centre in the federal provisions.
Eliminate option (b): Dyarchy was abolished at the provincial level — not retained or strengthened there under 1935.
Eliminate option (c): The 1919 Act had dyarchy only at the provincial level — it was never applied at the Centre under the 1919 Act.

Confirm option (d): The 1935 Act abolished dyarchy at the provincial level (provinces got full autonomy) and proposed dyarchy at the Centre as part of the federal structure — but this federal dyarchy was never implemented because the princely states did not accede.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students who know 'dyarchy was abolished under the 1935 Act' without knowing its full trajectory will miss the critical distinction: abolished at provincial level, proposed (but never implemented) at the Centre. The entity-swap trap operates by confusing the level (provincial vs central) at which dyarchy was maintained, shifted, or proposed.
solution.final_explanation:
Dyarchy's constitutional journey across the 1919 and 1935 Acts is a precise and frequently tested comparison.

• Option (a): Incorrect — dyarchy was not abolished entirely under the 1935 Act. Provincial dyarchy was abolished, but the 1935 Act proposed central dyarchy as part of the federal executive structure.
• Option (b): Incorrect — the 1935 Act specifically abolished dyarchy at the provincial level, replacing it with full provincial autonomy. Provincial ministers no longer had reserved subjects above them.
• Option (c): Incorrect — under the 1919 Act, dyarchy operated only at the provincial level. The Centre had no dyarchy — the Viceroy's Executive Council was entirely unaccountable to the legislature.
• Option (d): Correct — the 1935 Act abolished provincial dyarchy (provinces gained full autonomy) and proposed central dyarchy as part of the federal executive structure. However, this central dyarchy was never implemented because the required number of princely states did not accede to the All-India Federation.

Value Addition:
• Provincial autonomy under the 1935 Act came into force after the 1937 elections; Congress formed governments in 7 provinces.
• The federal provisions of the 1935 Act (including central dyarchy) never came into force due to the princely states' non-accession.
• The concept of dyarchy — divided executive — has no parallel in the 1950 Constitution, which established full parliamentary government.

solution.concept_anchor: Montagu Declaration: 'gradual development of self-governing institutions'
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is deceptive because 'responsible government for India as a Dominion' sounds like a natural culmination of the Declaration's aims, and students who associate the 1917 Declaration with a significant step forward may assume it used more ambitious language.
elimination_logic: The question asks for the exact qualifying language used in the Montagu Declaration of August 1917.
Eliminate option (a): 'Responsible government for India as a Dominion' — the Declaration did not promise Dominion Status. 'Dominion' does not appear in the 1917 Declaration.
Eliminate option (b): 'Immediate grant of representative institutions' — 'immediate' contradicts the Declaration's deliberate use of 'gradual.'
Confirm option (c): 'Gradual development of self-governing institutions' — 'gradual' was the operative qualifier, deliberately chosen to avoid any commitment to rapid transfer of power.
Eliminate option (d): 'Complete transfer of executive authority to elected legislatures' — far too broad and specific; the Declaration made no such commitment.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap operates through option (a) — 'Dominion' status sounds like a logical escalation from 'responsible government,' and students who know the Declaration used ambitious language may assume it went as far as Dominion Status. Critically, Dominion Status was the demand of the nationalist movement — not what the 1917 Declaration offered. The Declaration's language was carefully hedged with 'gradual,' which is the precise term UPSC tests.
solution.final_explanation:
The Montagu Declaration of August 1917 is significant as the first explicit British acknowledgment that responsible self-government for India was a policy objective — but its qualifying language was deliberately cautious.

• Option (a): 'Responsible government for India as a Dominion' — Incorrect. The Declaration did not use the word 'Dominion.' Dominion Status was the demand nationalists pressed for; the British explicitly declined to offer it in 1917.
• Option (b): 'Immediate grant of representative institutions' — Incorrect. 'Immediate' contradicts the exact language of the Declaration. The word 'gradual' was placed precisely to signal that any constitutional progress would be incremental and on British terms.
• Option (c): 'Gradual development of self-governing institutions' — Correct. This was the core phrase, accompanied by 'increasing association of Indians in every branch of the administration.' The word 'gradual' was the most debated element of the Declaration.
• Option (d): 'Complete transfer of executive authority to elected legislatures' — Incorrect. This level of commitment was never made in 1917; full executive accountability came only with the 1950 Constitution.

Value Addition:
• Full text of the key phrase: 'increasing association of Indians in every branch of the administration and the gradual development of self-governing institutions.'
• The Montagu Declaration is also called the 'August Declaration' of 1917.
• The gap between 'gradual development' (1917) and actual responsible government (1950) spans 33 years — a measure of how hedged the Declaration truly was.

• Universal women's franchise arrived only in 1950 with the Constitution of India.

solution.final_explanation:
Three dimensions of the 1919 Act are tested simultaneously in this question.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Edwin Montagu was Secretary of State for India; Lord Chelmsford was Viceroy of India. These two officials co-authored the Montagu-Chelmsford Report (1918) that became the basis for the Government of India Act 1919. Swapping their offices is the most common role-attribution error for this topic.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: 145 total members (105 elected) describes the Central Legislative Assembly (Lower House). The Council of State (Upper House) had 60 total members, of whom 27 were elected. Assigning the Lower House numbers to the Upper House is the numerical trap.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Morley-Minto Act (1909) retained an official nominated majority in provincial councils. The 1919 Act made elected members a majority — a significant structural shift, though qualified by the Governor's retained override powers.

Value Addition:
• The Council of State (Upper House) had higher property qualifications for voters and candidates — making it more conservative in composition.
• The Morley-Minto framework's official majority meant that even when Indians formed a plurality, they were outvoted by appointed officials.
• The 1919 Act's elected majority in provincial councils was a prerequisite for the ministerial accountability that dyarchy required.

Consider the following statements about the structural features of the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms:

1. The Montagu-Chelmsford Report of 1918, which formed the basis for the Government of India Act 1919, was co-authored by Edwin Montagu as Secretary of State for India and Lord Chelmsford as Viceroy of India.
2. The Council of State, introduced as the Upper House of the central legislature under the 1919 Act, had a total of 145 members of whom 105 were elected.
3. Under the Government of India Act 1919, elected members formed a majority in provincial legislative councils for the first time in colonial India's constitutional history.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?

(a) 1 only
(b) 2 and 3 only
(c) 1 and 3 only
(d) 1, 2 and 3
